newsitem.title: USA: NYC mayor and official feud over employees driving.
newsitem.headline: NYC mayor and official feud over employees driving.

text.p: The New York City mayor and comptroller on Friday feuded over a report by the financial watchdog that said unlicensed city workers, including police officers, were driving vehicles owned by the city.

Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, a Republican, on Friday implied that the study by the comptroller, Alan Hevesi, was partly motivated by political reasons. The comptroller, a Democrat, has said he expects to decide whether to run for mayor in the 1997 elections by the November U.S. Thanksgiving Day holiday.

"It's typical of Alan Hevesi, it's a cheap shot report. A lot of the numbers are wrong and I don't at this point expect anything better from Alan Hevesi than trying to fudge numbers in order to get himself on TV," Giuliani told reporters.
The two city officials have had a thorny relationship, and the comptroller has not hesitated to oppose the Giuliani Administration.

For example, Hevesi harshly criticized the mayor's 1997 fiscal budget, saying it failed to deal with the long-term and growing gap between revenues and expenditures. And the comptroller has won the opening rounds of a court battle to prevent the city from selling the water system.
In the latest controversy, Hevesi staunchly defended an audit by his staff that found about 1,200 city employees who were authorized to drive its vehicles did not have licenses.

"The mayor accuses me of trying to scare people with inflated numbers. His statement is false. We simply reported the numbers we found based on the information provided to us by the mayor's people," Hevesi said, in prepared remarks.

The police department led the comptroller's list with 361 unlicensed drivers, closely followed by the fire department, which had 241. Hevesi said that both agencies refused to document their data, adding only the police department disputed his findings.

In a June 4 response to Hevesi's findings, the police department said 248 of its employees who were identified by the comptroller had valid licenses and 50 were not required to drive, although 51 did have suspended licenses. And the licenses of a handful had been revoked.
Out of the pool of employees at all 31 agencies, 784 had been convicted for driving under the influence or while intoxicated, and 1,869 had had two or more accidents, Hevesi's audit found.

The police department said that only 19 of its current employees had been convicted of driving while intoxicated, less than half of the 58 identified by the comptroller, though two more employees are being probed as a result of the study.

Noting that one percent of the drivers identified in the comptroller's study caused 36 percent of the accidents, Hevesi added that claims soared to $30 million in fiscal year 1995, a 44 percent increase over the $21 million total in 1993.
